scenario: AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

message.reasoning:
The scenario describes a 33-year-old adult living with parents, paying $200 rent. The parents ask for help bringing in groceries; the person refuses, prioritizing a video game. This leads to a conflict, with parents leaving and demanding the person move out.

Key points:
- The person is an adult living with parents, paying below-market rent ($200 is very cheap).
- The parents request help with a household chore (groceries).
- The person refuses, claiming rent payment gives them privilege to say no.
- The refusal escalates to a shouting match, causing parents to leave and set an ultimatum.

Morally, the action of refusing to help with groceries when asked is questionable. While the person has a right to personal time, living with parents typically involves contributing to household tasks, especially when asked politely. The parents are providing housing at a very low cost, and helping with groceries is a reasonable expectation of shared living. The person's refusal, especially while playing a game and delaying repeatedly, shows a lack of consideration and respect. The escalation and parents' reaction indicate the refusal was a significant breach of mutual respect.

The person's justification that paying rent gives them privilege to say no is flawed; rent payment is for housing, not exemption from contributing to household responsibilities. In shared living, even with rent, there's an implicit or explicit agreement to help with chores. The person's avoidance and lack of engagement with parents further suggest a one-sided relationship.

Therefore, the action is morally unacceptable. The person should have helped, or at least communicated respectfully. The refusal led to conflict and consequences, highlighting the moral failing.
